transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-16
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Ethan (Redwood SE), Rina (Redwood CSM), Liam (Zephyr ML), Sara (Zephyr Platform), Priya (Zephyr CTO), Tom (Zephyr SRE)

Summary (auto): Quick review of last week's throughput runs; Ethan walked through staging logs and batch-size distributions; action to run a longer stress test and propose Dedicated concurrency settings.

[00:00] Maya (Redwood AE): alright everyone, thanks for jumping on. quick check - can you see my screen?
[00:06] Liam (Zephyr): yep, all good.
[00:10] Maya: awesome. quick agenda - recap the 1-hour run we did Friday, look at the continuous batching metrics, talk concurrency targets and queueing/backpressure, then decide next steps. Ethan, do you want to kick off with the run summary?
[00:22] Ethan (Redwood SE): sure. so from the friday run, staging at 1.2k RPS we saw average batch sizes around 8 to 12 requests per batch, average seq len about 320 tokens. latency p50 was 110ms, p95 around 420ms for the gen path. CPU/GPU utilization was stable, but we saw tail spikes when the request distribution changed - there was a small percent of long-context calls which blew up the KV cache misses. i want to call out that the continuous batching algorithm is doing what we expect: it forms batches opportunistically up to the target batch size, but if concurrency is too low we'll see small batches and higher per-token cost.
[01:05] Liam: okay, quick Q - that p95 of 420, is that including queueing time or just model time?
[01:10] Ethan: that's end-to-end from request ingress to token emission in staging; it includes queueing inside our request router and small backpressure windows. model time itself is more like p95 310ms.
[01:18] Sara: i'm seeing different numbers in our prod-like replay, we get p95 ~600ms at 1.2k RPS. might be because our payload distribution has more longer sequences.
[01:25] Ethan: yeah that aligns. you mentioned earlier you had a heavier tail on sequence lengths, that would increase batch variance and cause KV cache churn.
[01:33] Priya: can you remind us quickly what the KV cache miss impact is? we heard about it last week but want the concrete effect on throughput/cost.
[01:39] Ethan: sure - when KV cache hits are high, subsequent tokens avoid recomputing key/value layers and the runtime can serve with much higher tokens/sec. a miss forces recompute which increases GPU time per token by roughly 20-35% depending on sequence length and model. so hit rates matter a lot for steady throughput.
[01:55] Tom: do we have visibility into per-user or per-route cache locality? like if many of our users hit different contexts then we won't get the hit rates.
[02:02] Ethan: short answer, yes - we can surface per-route cache hit heatmaps. we looked at sample traffic and your route-a has about 70% hit rate, route-b much lower, ~28%. that's contributing to the tail.
[02:15] Maya: i wanted to pause and bring up concurrency targets - we've been conservative in the pilot at 16 concurrent workers in the Dedicated pool. that keeps latency stable but underutilizes batching. if we bump concurrency to 48 or 64, continuous batching fills larger batches and lowers per-token cost, but obviously the p95 can drift if you get a lot of long requests.
[02:39] Sara: what's the recommended concurrency range for a mix like ours? we have bursty traffic but median seq len around 220 and 10% long sessions >1k tokens.
[02:47] Ethan: for that profile i'd aim for 48 concurrency as a starting point with a soft cap and queueing thresholds. the approach we've used successfully: set target_concurrency=48, queue_depth=200 and enable adaptive backpressure so that very long requests can be routed to a smaller pool or fall back to a less expensive variant.
[03:06] Liam: can you explain adaptive backpressure? i think we saw that term but not the mechanics.
[03:10] Ethan: yeah, adaptive backpressure is the router-level policy - when queue depth exceeds a threshold, new requests are either queued with an estimate or forwarded to a fallback model (a smaller/quantized variant) or rejected with a retry-after header. it's tunable by traffic class. it helps protect latency SLOs for the majority of requests.
[03:29] Priya: hm - fallback to a quantized model could affect quality. how do we measure regressions?
[03:33] Maya: good callout. we pair fallback with quick evals on key prompts and have an A/B canary route where 10% of traffic gets the fallback and we monitor quality deltas. for you guys we suggested a 1% canary then scale if quality is acceptable.
[03:49] Tom: what's the expected cost delta if we increase concurrency versus staying low and relying on burst capacity?
[03:54] Ethan: roughly speaking, increasing concurrency improves GPU utilization so per-token cost drops 15-30% depending on batch sizes. however, if you need bigger Dedicated fleet to sustain higher concurrency across peak windows, there's an infra cost. our Optimize team models it: for your current workload moving from 16 to 48 concurrency we estimate a net 12% reduction in token cost after amortizing infra. we'll put the spreadsheet in the drive.
[04:18] Sara: okay, can you show the batch size distribution from the Friday run?
[04:21] Ethan: pulling it up - here's the histogram. you can see a mode at 9 requests/batch but a long left tail with single-request batches. that's the inefficiency.
[04:30] Liam: those single-request batches - are they timed out because of per-request latency constraints?
[04:34] Ethan: yes, the runtime has a max_batch_latency parameter (we had it at 8ms in staging). increasing that to 16-20ms allows more requests to accumulate but adds a small fixed latency per request. it's a tradeoff.
[04:46] Maya: in practice we've found increasing max_batch_latency to 12-15ms often yields bigger batches with minimal user-visible impact. worth testing for you since your p50s are already relatively low.
[04:55] Priya: can we do an experiment where we vary max_batch_latency and concurrency in a planned test matrix? say 3x2 - low/med/high concurrency x two latency windows?
[05:03] Ethan: absolutely. we can run a sweep in staging and then you can replicate in prod-replay. i'll prepare the matrix and expected metrics.
[05:10] Rina (CSM): i'll coordinate the schedule and collect the results into a single sheet so we can compare.
[05:15] Sara: about queueing - is there risk of head-of-line blocking? if a very long request occupies the model, does it block smaller ones?
[05:21] Ethan: the runtime isolates KV cache per-request and uses sharded execution; but yes, long sequence requests can increase tail latency for other requests if concurrency is low. that's why we recommend per-class routing and sometimes dedicating a small subset of capacity to long-running jobs.
[05:34] Liam: curious - what's the easiest way for us to measure per-route hit rates and batch composition?
[05:38] Maya: we'll share the dashboard link - it surfaces per-route batch size, kv hit rate, gpu utilization, and token cost. also a CSV export.
[05:45] Tom: for the stress test, do you have a recommended traffic pattern? we want it to be realistic with bursts and some long-tail.
[05:51] Ethan: recommended pattern attached in the runbook - it includes a base traffic of 1.2k RPS, bursts to 2k RPS for 5 minutes every 15 minutes, and 10% long requests interspersed. also seed with route-b heavy tail for 25% of traffic to hit the low-hit scenario.
[06:09] Priya: on security and logs - can you confirm logs won't include PII? we need masked traces.
[06:14] Maya: yes, logs can be configured to redact or not store payloads; by default pilot logs are redacted and we can enable token-level audit on request if you approve.
[06:23] Sara: one more - quantization. you mentioned earlier the Optimize team had suggestions. given our token distribution, would q4_0 or int8 give acceptable quality?
[06:30] Ethan: initial hope is int8 fastpath might be fine for most routes; for high-quality routes we'll recommend a mixed strategy - int8 for inference-heavy, float16 for quality-critical. we'll need your sample payloads to run evals.
[06:41] Liam: ok, good. for the immediate next step we will run the 2-hour stress test. what do you need from us right now to set it up?
[06:47] Maya: the runbook, traffic harness link, and a single test account to authenticate. also export of your sample payloads and route mapping. we'll loop in SRE for the schedules.
[06:58] Liam: we'll have that by EOD monday.
[07:01] Maya: great. final quick recap: Ethan will prepare concurrency+latency sweep matrix; Maya will upload throughput spreadsheet and runbook; Zephyr will run 2-hour stress and provide payload samples; Rina will schedule follow-up. any objections?
[07:12] Priya: none here. thanks.
[07:15] Tom: sounds good. one last question - if after test we need Dedicated capacity changes, what's lead time?
[07:20] Maya: for pilot fleets we can provision extra Dedicated nodes within 48-72 hours; for a longer term commit we'll discuss capacity planning but pilot bursts are quick.
[07:29] Sara: ok thanks everyone.
[07:32] Maya: thanks all, we'll follow up with the spreadsheet and runbook.
[07:36] (meeting ends)

Notes: Transcript contains occasional mis-transcriptions (e.g., 'kay-vee cache' for KV cache). References: benchmark spreadsheet (link shared in chat), runbook and stress harness (drive link), security docs (redwood/security.pdf).
